title: Check Substring
directAnswer: Use `s.contains(sub)` / `sub in s`. To show the algorithm, check each start index `i` in `0..n-m` and compare the m characters. O(n·m) naive.

remember.takeaway: Substring search is window matching; KMP makes it linear.
remember.formula: for i in 0..n-m: if s[i:i+m]==sub return true; (empty -> true)
antiSignals: Very large inputs — use KMP/Z-algorithm for O(n+m)

problemStatement: Given two strings `s` and `sub`, return whether `sub` occurs somewhere inside `s` as a contiguous substring.
understanding: Slide a window of length |sub| across s and compare; or use the built-in contains/indexOf.

approaches.name: Sliding window compare
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Decide whether `sub` occurs inside `s`. The library way is `s.contains(sub)`; the algorithmic way is a sliding-window compare: at each start index in s, check whether the next |sub| characters match.

**Why O(n·m) naive.** There are up to n−m+1 start positions, and each comparison can take up to m characters, so the brute force is O(n·m). It's fine for fresher scope, but name the upgrade.

**The empty-needle convention.** An empty `sub` is a substring of every string (it 'occurs' at position 0), so return true for it. Mishandling this is a common edge-case slip.

**The linear upgrade.** KMP precomputes a failure function so it never re-compares characters, achieving O(n+m); `indexOf`/`contains` are typically optimised similarly. Mentioning KMP shows you know the brute force isn't optimal.

code.python:
def contains(s: str, sub: str) -> bool:
    return sub in s
